one_line: Fuel droplets about 4 mm across were burned in a sealed chamber on the ISS to study 'cool flames': invisible, low-temperature flames (roughly 700-900 K) that keep a droplet burning after its normal hot flame has gone out.
summary: CFI burned about 4 mm droplets of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane blends (75/25 and 60/40 by mass) and farnesane in the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus on the ISS in 2017, at 0.5-5 atm (51-507 kPa), 17-21% O2 and 0-59% helium. More than two hundred tests were run. Large droplets first burned with a hot flame that went out by radiative heat loss after about 10-14 s in air. A cool flame then kept the droplet burning quasi-steadily, close to the droplet, until it too extinguished at a finite diameter and left a cloud of condensed, partly oxidised vapour. For n-dodecane in air the cool-flame extinction diameter fell from about 1.7-1.9 mm at 0.5 atm to below 0.4 mm at 1.25 atm. Helium dilution increased it, to 2.1-2.6 mm with 59% helium at 1 atm. Iso-dodecane suppressed cool flames. At 2 atm and above, cool flames repeatedly re-ignited hot flames. For spacecraft fire safety, this means a fuel can keep reacting, and producing flammable vapour, after the visible flame has gone out.

question.text: FLEX and FLEX-2 had found, by accident, that large n-alkane droplets keep burning quasi-steadily after their hot flame is extinguished by radiation, supported by low-temperature ('cool flame') chemistry in the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) range. CFI set out to study this regime systematically. It asked how fuel structure (n-dodecane, branched iso-dodecane in blends, and the renewable fuel farnesane), ambient pressure (0.5-5 atm) and helium dilution change the hot-flame and cool-flame burning rates, flame sizes, radiant output and, above all, the droplet diameter at cool-flame extinction. That diameter gives a measure of low-temperature chemical time scales that can be used to test and improve kinetic mechanisms. A secondary aim was to understand soot behaviour during cool-flame burning.

sources.quote: The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.”
the droplet extinction diameter provides a stringent measurement of chemical-kinetic characteristic times.
Examine the cool flame combustion behavior of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane fuel mixtures, and farnesane fuels over a rage of pressure from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.

The overall goal of the proposed experiments is to improve our understanding of low temperature chemistry by studying the cool flame burning and, most importantly, cool flame extinction of droplet burning with spherical symmetry in a long-duration microgravity environment.

physics.text: Alkane oxidation follows different chemical routes at different temperatures. Below about 900 K, chain branching runs through peroxy radicals (RO2, QOOH, O2QOOH) and ketohydroperoxides. As temperature rises through the NTC region the overall rate falls, because these intermediates dissociate back, before high-temperature branching takes over above about 1100-1200 K. A spherically symmetric droplet diffusion flame normally burns in the high-temperature branch, and its flame radius is many droplet diameters. A large droplet in microgravity has a large flame whose radiative loss scales with flame volume, while heat release scales only with droplet diameter, so it can extinguish radiatively. In FLEX and CFI the gas left near the droplet after this extinction is hot enough for low-temperature chemistry to ignite a 'cool' diffusion flame at roughly 700-900 K. This flame sits close to the droplet (flame standoff ratio about 3) and releases roughly half the heat. It burns quasi-steadily, following a d-squared law, until the residence time in the reaction zone, which shrinks with droplet size, falls below the chemical time at the lower turning point of the NTC branch, and the flame goes out. Pressure shortens chemical times, so it lowers the extinction diameter. Helium raises thermal diffusivity and heat loss, so it raises the extinction diameter. Branched isomers form fewer of the five- and six-membered ring transition states needed for low-temperature branching, so they weaken cool flames. On Earth, buoyant convection on mm-size droplets is far faster than diffusion, so neither the spherical symmetry nor the long residence times these flames need can be achieved. Drop towers are also too short to reach radiative extinction.

sources.quote: FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K.
In microgravity where the buoyancy-induced flow is absent, larger droplets can extinguish as a result of the ex- cessive radiant heat loss from the flame zone (Chao et al., 1991).

The heat release during this second-stage burning is approximately half of what is normally associated with n-heptane combustion and the activation energy associated with the chemical processes is similar to that of low-temperature ignition chemistry Nayagam et al. (2012).

As the droplet size decreases, the residence time in the reaction zone of the gas-phase diffusion flame is reduced to a value corresponding to which the cool flame becomes statically unstable, and this leads to cool flame extinction.

equations.meaning: Quasi-steady d-squared law. D is droplet diameter (mm), D_0 the initial diameter (mm), t time since ignition (s), k the burning-rate constant (mm^2/s). CFI fits k separately for the hot-flame stage (k_hot) and the cool-flame stage (k_cool), over roughly 0.1-0.9 of each stage. Valid for spherically symmetric, quasi-steady burning; it fails during ignition transients, re-ignition and on a disturbed fibre.

sources.quote: The average burning rate constant (¯k) comes from a linear fit of the droplet-squared history between approximately t = 0.1τb and 0.9τb, where τb is the total burn time (igniter withdraw to extinction or burnout).

equations.meaning: Droplet lifetime (s) from the initial diameter D_0 (mm) and the average burning-rate constant k (mm^2/s). For D_0 = 3-6 mm and k = 0.5 mm^2/s this is 18-72 s, far longer than drop-tower times (up to about 5-10 s). That is why the ISS is needed.

sources.quote: Typically the droplet life-time (τl) can be estimated from the initial droplet size (D0) and the average burning rate constant (k) as τl = D2 0 k .

equations.meaning: Ratios of thermal (tau_k) and mass (tau_m) diffusion times to the buoyant residence time tau_b, for droplet diameter D (m), gravity g (m/s^2), gas thermal diffusivity alpha_g and mass diffusivity D_g (m^2/s). Both ratios must be much less than 1 for buoyancy to be negligible and the flame spherical. At 1 g and 1 atm this needs D much smaller than 1 mm, below cool-flame extinction diameters. Diffusivities scale as 1/p, so higher pressure makes buoyancy worse.

sources.quote: In order to justify neglecting buoyant effects the above ratios must be much lower than unity.

equations.meaning: Yang-Gray thermokinetic condition for an NTC region. In the scheme A -> X (initiation), X -> 2X (branching, activation energy E_b), X -> products (low-temperature termination E_t1, high-temperature termination E_t2), the overall rate falls with rising temperature over a range when this ordering holds. It is a conceptual model, not quantitative for real fuels.

sources.quote: They showed that for this scheme the NTC region is possible when the activation energies obey the following condition: Et1 <Eb <Et2.

equations.meaning: Scaling behind radiative extinction. Radiative loss from the flame grows with flame volume (r_f = flame radius), while heat release grows only linearly with droplet diameter D. Large droplets (and large flames in microgravity) therefore lose a growing fraction of their heat and extinguish radiatively. This sets up the cool-flame stage. Qualitative scaling for optically thin gas radiation.

sources.quote: the rate of radiant loss (proportional to the flame vol- ume) increases faster than the rate of heat release (proportional to the droplet diameter).

apparatus.text: The CIR provides a 90 l combustion chamber (rated to about 9 atm; CFI went to 5 atm), gas mixing (FOMA), pressure and temperature sensors, and imaging. It is vibration-isolated by PaRIS (Passive Rack Isolation System), and g-levels were typically below 1e-5 g0. The MDCA deploys a droplet by dispensing fuel between two opposed 250 um outside-diameter needles, stretching it, then retracting the needles quickly. CFI used a thinner 40 um SiC tether fibre than FLEX's 80 um fibre, to keep droplets in view while disturbing them less near cool-flame extinction. Two hot-wire igniters (about 12-13 W, 1-11 s on-time) were positioned near the droplet and withdrawn once it ignited. Diagnostics: a backlit (red laser-diode) HiBMS camera at 30 frames/s for droplet diameter; an intensified camera with hot-flame and cool-flame modes for OH* and cool-flame imaging; a colour camera with live downlink; and a radiometer package with a wideband channel (0.6-10 um, mainly hot flame) and a narrowband channel (5.0-6.5 um water band, sensitive to the cool flame) sampled at 100 Hz. Chamber pressures and four temperatures were logged throughout. The CFI requirements asked for larger fields of view than FLEX (50 mm droplet view, 80 mm flame view) and auto-gain radiometers.

procedure.text: The crew installed fuel syringes and gas bottles. Everything else was run from the Telescience Support Center at NASA GRC. For each test day the chamber was filled with the chosen O2/N2(/He) mixture and pressure and left about 2 minutes to settle. A set amount of fuel was then dispensed between the needles (or onto the fibre), stretched, and deployed. After a dwell of at least 10 s the igniters were powered for a preset time (1-5 s planned; later raised, e.g. to 8 s after a software change), then withdrawn. Cameras and radiometers recorded the hot-flame burn, its extinction, cool-flame burning, cool-flame extinction and vapour-cloud formation. A fan then mixed the chamber for about 15 s. Typically 5-10 droplets of different sizes were burned per atmosphere, about 8 per day, with later tests guided by earlier results. Data were downlinked and reduced to droplet diameter-squared histories (equivalent-area diameter of the backlit droplet), hot- and cool-flame diameters (FWHM and peak-to-peak of the cool-flame intensity profile), burning-rate constants from linear fits, extinction diameters and radiance traces.

psi_data.summary: PSI-39 holds 2,832 files (about 719 GB), 2,125 of them downloaded locally. Nearly all the volume is Raw Data (2,791 files, 718.9 GB): 337 zip image archives (588.9 GB), one per camera stream per test point for 85 test points, with suffixes A, C, D, G and a few S/I; 120 .ts and 126 .mp4 downlink video recordings (109.8 and 18.9 GB); and 1,793 small text files. For each of about 123 CIR test points (CIR ids such as F068A03) there are: test-point settings (igniter power and on-time, needle and igniter positions, dispensed volume), camera settings, filter and CFI-mode logs, chamber readings (pressures in psia and temperatures in deg C, about 1 Hz), radiometer readings, image timing indexes, and a 'Comments' file. The Comments files are data-integrity logs (missing image files, bad frame intervals, re-downlinks), not science notes. For a subset of tests there are reduced text files (FLEX-xxxx_DropletData, RadiometerData, ColorCamData, CoolFlameData, TestSheet), 22 RTF test sheets and 28 Igor .pxp analysis files. The most usable products are the Jan 2021 data-summary spreadsheet, which gives 227 test conditions, and for 146 analysed tests D0, extinction diameters, k_hot, k_cool, re-ignition counts, burn time and peak radiances, with operator comments per test; and 30 Analyzed Data PDFs (FLEX-1206 to 1264 and 1393), each a one-page plot of droplet, flame and radiance histories. The 87-row experimental table is a partial subset of the spreadsheet's Master Sheet.

findings.claim: With pure n-dodecane in air (21% O2, balance N2), droplets of about 3.8-4.7 mm at 0.5-1.25 atm burned first with a hot flame. The flame went out by radiative extinction after about 10-14 s (up to 17 s), with the droplet at about 2.9-4.3 mm. Quasi-steady cool-flame burning usually followed, often ending with a large vapour cloud. Not every test shows this: FLEX-1207 to 1210 have no cool-flame extinction diameter, the FLEX-1207 comment notes no large vapour cloud, and the FLEX-1222 comment says the flame burned to completion. The cool-flame burning-rate constant (0.31-0.43 mm^2/s) was about the same as the hot-flame value (0.30-0.52 mm^2/s).

sources.quote: Excellent deployment. Ignition just before igniters pull away. Droplet drifts W in color camera FOV but stays in FOV the entire time. Hot flame extinguishers without oscillations. Long cool flame burn with large vapor cloud.

findings.claim: For n-dodecane in air the cool-flame extinction diameter falls steeply with pressure. It was 1.73-1.92 mm at 0.5 atm (50.7 kPa; 5 tests), 0.68-1.14 mm at 0.75 atm (76 kPa; 5 tests), mostly 0.26-0.85 mm at 1 atm (101 kPa; one outlier of 2.97 mm in FLEX-1251), and 0-0.39 mm at 1.25 atm (127 kPa). At 2-5 atm most droplets left no measurable residual droplet (recorded as 0 mm). The investigators note that simplified chemistry predicts these diameters less well as pressure rises.

findings.claim: Above about 2 atm the cool flame often re-ignited a hot flame, sometimes repeatedly. The sequence was hot flame, radiative extinction, cool flame, hot re-ignition, cool flame again, until the fuel was used up. No n-dodecane test at 0.5-1.25 atm re-ignited. In the spreadsheet, re-ignitions are logged for all 4 n-dodecane tests in air at 2 atm (FLEX-1227 twice, 1228-1230 once each) and for up to 7 cycles in one 3 atm test (FLEX-1258, D0 = 5.5 mm). The investigators had not expected this from FLEX. Under fire-safety applications, a CFI presentation notes that in space a persisting cool flame can generate combustible vapour that can re-ignite.

sources.quote: However, as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed.
This behavior is unexpected based on earlier observations from FLEX experiments.

findings.claim: Helium dilution at 21% O2 shortened the hot flame and enlarged the cool-flame extinction diameter. At 1 atm, n-dodecane extinction diameters were 0.90-0.97 mm with 29% helium (vs mostly 0.26-0.85 mm without) and 2.10-2.57 mm with 59% helium. Hot-flame burn time fell from about 10-12 s in air to about 7 s at 29% helium and 1.9-3 s at 59% helium. In FLEX-1281 (59% He, 1 atm) the hot flame existed only while the igniters were on.

findings.claim: Adding iso-dodecane suppressed cool flames, most clearly in the 60/40 blend at low pressure. At 0.5-0.75 atm in air, 60/40 droplets had cool-flame burning-rate constants of only 0.10-0.23 mm^2/s, against 0.31-0.37 for pure n-dodecane, and cool-flame 'extinction' diameters of 3.8-5.6 mm, within about 0.1 mm of their hot-flame extinction diameters. In other words, the cool flame barely lasted. The 75/25 blend at 0.75 atm behaved more like pure n-dodecane (extinction diameters 0.48 and 0.90 mm).

sources.quote: The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol.

findings.claim: At 17% O2 and 1 atm the hot flame was weak and short-lived: 4.7-7.2 s for n-dodecane and 3.3-4.7 s for the blends, with hot-flame burning-rate constants often below 0.1 mm^2/s for the blends. Pure n-dodecane still showed cool-flame burning, with larger extinction diameters (1.27-2.87 mm) than in air. Most blend tests at 17% O2 and 1 atm have no cool-flame burning rate in the spreadsheet; one 75/25 test extinguished at 4.35 mm.

findings.claim: At higher pressure (for example n-dodecane at 3 atm with 29% He, FLEX-1268), radiative extinction was followed by an intermediate 'warm flame', not visible on the colour camera. A hot flame then re-ignited and quickly went out to a cool flame. The investigators attribute warm flames to intermediate-temperature chemistry becoming active, and report that helium appears to help the heat-release/heat-loss balance in the NTC region. Sources conflict on the FLEX-1268 atmosphere: the Final Report's Figure 3 caption gives 12% O2/50% N2/29% He, while the data-summary spreadsheet (Master Sheet) gives O2 0.21, N2 0.50, He 0.29. The caption's 12% is probably a typo for 21%, since 12 + 50 + 29 = 91%.

relevance.text: CFI is a fundamental combustion-chemistry experiment, not a material-flammability test, but it points to a spacecraft fire hazard. In microgravity, a burning liquid fuel (or, by analogy, a fuel-soaked object) whose visible flame has gone out can keep reacting through an invisible cool flame at about 700-900 K. That flame gasifies the fuel at nearly the hot-flame rate and leaves a cloud of fuel vapour and partly oxidised products. At 2 atm and above it repeatedly re-ignited hot flames, and a FLEX re-ignition burned brighter than the original flame, consistent with a premixed flame through the accumulated vapour. Detection and extinguishment criteria based only on visible flame or hot-flame radiation may therefore declare a fire out too early. The narrowband water-vapour radiometer did detect cool flames. Helium dilution and lower O2 shortened hot flames but increased the cool-flame extinction diameter, so inert agents change how much liquid is left unburned and vaporising.

sources.quote: Since the cool flame mode of droplet combustion can persist after hot-flame extinction (and may even transition back to hot flaming under certain conditions), safety procedures based only on considerations of hot flame properties or sensing may be inadequate for assuring safety under all conditions.

sources.file: PSI-39_Presentations_Cool Flames in Space, a Hot Prospect on Earth_CFI.pdf
sources.quote: These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments

This suggests that the reignited hot flame is either a pre-mixed or partially pre-mixed flame propagating through the fuel vapor/air mixture that results from the unconsumed fuel during the cool flame period mixing with ambient air.
The new radiometers, particularly the narrowband radiometer, were sensitive to the cool flame and could detect both the cool flame burning and, most importantly, the cool flame extinction.

habitat_conditions.text: CFI used only 17% and 21% O2, with N2 or N2/He diluent, at 0.5-5 atm (50.7-506.6 kPa). The 21% O2, 1 atm tests match the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa). No test used the elevated-O2, reduced-pressure atmospheres planned for exploration: the Moon-habitat reference is 30% or more O2 at 70.3 kPa or less, and the spacesuit reference is 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa. The 0.5 and 0.75 atm air tests (O2 partial pressure about 10.7 and 16 kPa) are closest in total pressure to a habitat, but have much lower oxygen partial pressure. The low-pressure trend (larger cool-flame extinction diameter and slower cool-flame burning as pressure falls) suggests cool flames would be shorter-lived at habitat pressure, but the effect of 30% O2 was not measured. The SRD planned O2 up to 0.35-0.40 and xenon diluent, but these were not in the flown matrix. The predecessor FLEX tested a 30/70 O2/N2 pre-EVA atmosphere at 0.7 atm.

earth_benefits.text: Data for validating low-temperature (NTC) chemical kinetic mechanisms for n-dodecane, a jet/diesel surrogate component, its branched isomer and the renewable fuel farnesane. These mechanisms underpin autoignition, knock, octane and cetane behaviour and the design of low-temperature engines (HCCI, RCCI). Other suggested applications are cool-flame fuel reforming (for example hydrogen for fuel cells) and new spray-burner concepts.

sources.quote: The CFI experimental measurements provide a useful way to validate the complex chemical kinetic mechanisms that are being developed. The cool flame combustion process itself maybe of use in fuel reformulation technologies to produce hydrogen in fuel cell applications.

limitations.text: By the final report (July 2020) the investigators had not fully analysed or modelled the CFI data. Findings are 'general observations' from preliminary analysis. The spreadsheet marks 81 of 227 test points as not analysed, including all 44 farnesane tests and all 75/25 blend tests with helium.

sources.quote: All the CFI data is yet to be fully analyzed and interpreted using theoretical and numerical models.

limitations.text: Droplet ignition used hot wires and a strong ignition stimulus. Cool flames in this configuration occur almost only after radiative extinction of a large (about 4 mm) droplet's hot flame, so the results describe large isolated droplets in a quiescent gas. They do not describe sprays, pools, wicks or ventilated cabins.

open_questions: Fit the n-dodecane cool-flame extinction diameter against pressure (0.5-5 atm), O2 (0.17, 0.21) and helium (0-0.59) from the DATA sheet, and compare with the Williams-Nayagam simplified chemistry and with detailed mechanisms to quantify the pressure deterioration they report.

Analyse the 44 farnesane tests (FLEX-1388 to 1431), which have raw data but no reduced values in the spreadsheet, and compare cool-flame burning rates and extinction diameters with n-dodecane against cetane number (58 vs 78).

Use the narrowband water-band radiometer records to build an objective cool-flame-presence and extinction detector, and test whether a fire sensor could flag invisible cool-flame burning after visible extinction.

Quantify the re-ignition period and the number of cycles against pressure, droplet size and helium fraction (Reignitions column plus radiometer traces), and estimate the fuel vapour mass accumulated before each re-ignition.
Measure soot-shell diameter and its loss of definition with pressure from the backlit images, to address the unexplained high-pressure soot behaviour.
Separate fibre and free-droplet effects on k_cool and extinction diameter across all conditions using the Fiber column.

gaps: Dates conflict. The PSI record gives investigationStartDate 10-01-2020 and investigationEndDate 10-20-2021. The experimental table and data-summary spreadsheet date the tests 9 Mar 2017 to 15 Sep 2017. The Final Report (dated 23 Jul 2020) says operations ran from January 2017 through September 2017. The record uses the dated test span (2017-03-09 to 2017-09-15). The 2020-2021 PSI dates may refer to a data-processing or archiving period; no document explains them.

The spreadsheet Master Sheet dates FLEX-1411 (farnesane) to 2011-09-06, which is clearly a typing error for 2017 (neighbouring tests are August-September 2017). The tests table now corrects it to 2017-09-06 using its CIR code.

The experimental table CSV (87 rows) lists FLEX-1285-1289 and 1295-1297 twice, so it has only 79 unique tests. It omits all farnesane tests and pure-dodecane tests at 0.5, 0.75, 3 and 5 atm and with helium. FLEX-1219 to 1222 list O2 0.21 + N2 0.76 (sum 0.97). Pressure strings carry trailing spaces. The full 227-row list is in the data-summary spreadsheet, which was read directly; facts from rows beyond its preview are cited as psi_table.

The PSI record's approach says the chamber pressure ranged from 0.25 to 0.5 atm, and its objective and the Final Report mention 0.25 atm. No test below 0.5 atm appears in the table or spreadsheet, and the Operational Requirements give 0.5-5.0 atm. The approach also calls nitrogen 'atomic nitrogen' (it is N2).

The Final Report text says 'n-dodecanol' and 'iso-dodecanol' in section 5.1, which are evidently typos for n-dodecane and iso-dodecane (its figure captions and all data use the alkanes). The PSI record hypothesis says 'faresane' for farnesane.
The SRD says the initial chamber temperature will be 'around 250 C'. This is presumably a typo for about 25 C: the FLEX-1206 test sheet logs 299.19 K and the chamber readings about 24-27 C.
The PSI record contact list gives D. Dietrich's email with a misspelled surname; contact emails were not copied into this record.

The Final Report figures (cool-flame extinction diameter vs pressure; helium effect; backlit soot images) have no text layer for the plotted values, and the PDF pages could not be rendered here (no poppler). Values were taken from the data-summary spreadsheet instead. FLEX-1248_Summary.pdf failed text extraction (PdfStreamError).

The main CFI results paper (Dietrich et al. 2024, Microgravity Sci. Technol., doi 10.1007/s12217-024-10115-x) is closed access, and its abstract is not available from Springer, Crossref or Semantic Scholar. Its results are not included. The 2020 ASGSR abstract on NTRS and the Williams and Nayagam 2020 Combustion and Flame abstract were reachable and are cited.

Raw image zips, .ts and .mp4 videos (about 718 GB) were not inspected. The per-test 'Comments.txt' raw files sampled (e.g. F068A03, F160A03, F180D04) contain only image-integrity logs, not science observations. Science observations are in the spreadsheet Comments sheet.

The two presentations (2013, 2015) predate CFI flight and describe FLEX cool-flame results and theory (partial-burning regime, flame standoff ratio about 3.1, extinction correlated with oxygen concentration to the -3/2 power). They give no CFI data.

No 30-day operational accomplishments report exists (the Final Report appendix says 'Not available'). The Final Report gives the PSI data organisation as FLEX-1206 to 1284 (n-dodecane), 1285 to 1387 (blends) and 1388 to 1431 (farnesane).

Publication review (Nov 2026; per-paper notes in data/publications/PSI-39.json): of the 7 listed publications, 1 was read in full (NTRS preprint of Nayagam et al. 2015), 3 by abstract and 3 not at all (Nayagam et al. 2012 Combustion and Flame, the 2024 CFI results paper, and the NASA blog post "Science in Short: Cool Flames", whose URL now redirects and whose archived copy refused automated access). The readable papers analyse FLEX/FLEX-2 n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane data from before CFI; none adds CFI-specific results to this record.
